positioning: The open-source coordination layer for parallel agentic development.
headline: Run agents in parallel. Build as a team.

phases.label: Record
phases.title: Local work is recorded.
phases.body: L1 reports activity in billing.mjs. Local sessions keep their own host permissions.

phases.label: Publish
phases.title: Share metadata through Git.
phases.body: With remote sharing enabled, LangSpan publishes branch and file activity, not source contents.

phases.label: Brief
phases.title: Related work reaches the next prompt.
phases.body: C1 can receive relevant peer context. Its own coordinator handles local work; remote awareness does not lock its files.

topology.boundary: Illustrated topology inspired by five local and five cloud sessions. Not a measured LangSpan scale test.

beats.label: Independent edits
beats.title: Two useful changes, separately.
beats.result: Both branches pass their own tests.
beats.description: One agent renames an export. Another adds a caller on a separate branch, based on the old interface.

beats.label: Clean merge
beats.title: Git merges. The build breaks.
beats.description: There are no overlapping file edits. A combined check catches the incompatible interface.

beats.label: Coordinate & verify
beats.title: Make the related work visible.
beats.description: A relevant briefing can surface the changed file. The agent still has to inspect it, choose a compatible edit and pass the combined check.

semantic.boundary: The Git example is scripted; no model runs. The briefing-assisted recovery is an illustration, not an observed LangSpan outcome.

research.name: CooperBench
research.desc: Average success rate for cooperating agents versus completing both tasks individually in a collaborative coding benchmark.

research.name: ParallACT
research.desc: Success on contradictory tasks: one Claude Code agent given both tasks versus two agents working independently (Opus 4.8).

research.name: Worse Together
research.desc: Simulated environments in which separate agents produced worse group outcomes than a single coordinator.
